clique_expansion(): projecting back, and what it costs

honets

2026-08-26

The analytic question

Most network tools take a pairwise network. clique_expansion() turns a hypergraph into one, so the whole first-order toolkit becomes available — plotting, community detection, standard centralities.

It is also the clearest way to see what a hypergraph representation is worth, because the projection is lossy and irreversible, and you can measure exactly how much it throws away.

library(honets)
library(cograph)

Projecting

Every pair of nodes sharing a hyperedge gets an edge, weighted by how much they share.

hg <- group_hypergraph(human_long, member = "code", group = "session_id")
net <- clique_expansion(hg)
class(net)
[1] "netobject"       "cograph_network"
c(nodes = net$n_nodes, edges = net$n_edges)
nodes edges 
    9    36 
round(net$weights[1:5, 1:5])
          Command Correct Frustrate Inquire Interrupt
Command         0     267       250     261       390
Correct       267       0       184     189       249
Frustrate     250     184         0     179       245
Inquire       261     189       179       0       253
Interrupt     390     249       245     253         0

Nine nodes, 36 edges — the complete graph on nine nodes. Command and Interrupt share 390 sessions; Frustrate and Inquire share 179.

The return is a netobject / cograph_network, so it drops straight into the packages that consume those.

What weighted actually controls

It binarises the incidence, not the output. The output is always a count of shared hyperedges (weighted by incidence values when they exist).

dw <- data.frame(member = c("A", "B", "C", "A", "B"),
                 grp    = c("g1", "g1", "g1", "g2", "g2"),
                 n      = c(2, 5, 3, 1, 4), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
hw <- group_hypergraph(dw, member = "member", group = "grp", weight = "n")
hw$incidence
  g1 g2
A  2  1
B  5  4
C  3  0
clique_expansion(hw, weighted = TRUE)$weights
   A  B  C
A  0 14  6
B 14  0 15
C  6 15  0
clique_expansion(hw, weighted = FALSE)$weights
  A B C
A 0 2 1
B 2 0 1
C 1 1 0

With TRUE, A-B is 2×5 + 1×4 = 14 — the incidence values multiply. With FALSE, A-B is 2 — they simply share two hyperedges.

On a hypergraph whose incidence is already 0/1 the argument does nothing:

hb <- group_hypergraph(dw, member = "member", group = "grp")
identical(clique_expansion(hb, weighted = TRUE)$weights,
          clique_expansion(hb, weighted = FALSE)$weights)
[1] TRUE

Seeing the projection

The projected object is a cograph_network, so it plots directly — which is most of the reason to project at all.

splot(net, minimum = 0.05, title = "Hypergraph, projected")

The information the projection destroys

This is the part worth internalising. Take a hypergraph with two 3-groups, project it, and rebuild a hypergraph from the projection:

d <- data.frame(member = c("A", "B", "C", "A", "B", "D"),
                grp    = c("g1", "g1", "g1", "g2", "g2", "g2"),
                stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
h1 <- group_hypergraph(d, member = "member", group = "grp")
as.data.frame(h1)$states
[1] "A, B, C" "A, B, D"

Two genuine three-way groups. Project:

n1 <- clique_expansion(h1)
n1$weights
  A B C D
A 0 2 1 1
B 2 0 1 1
C 1 1 0 0
D 1 1 0 0

Rebuild:

h2 <- build_hypergraph(n1$weights, threshold = 0)
as.data.frame(h2)$states
[1] "A, B"    "A, D"    "B, D"    "A, C"    "B, C"    "A, B, D" "A, B, C"

Two hyperedges went in; seven came out. The two real triples are recovered — but so are five pairwise edges that were never groups in their own right, only by-products of the projection. A hypergraph and its projection are not interchangeable, and the round trip cannot tell a genuine group from a triangle of coincidences.

That gap is the entire case for build_hypergraph()’s p parameter: when you must infer groups from pairwise data, p is where you state how much you believe the inference.

Projecting collapses the coding sessions completely

m <- hypergraph_measures(hg)
as.data.frame(m, what = "global")
                 measure       value
1                n_nodes   9.0000000
2           n_hyperedges 429.0000000
3                density   0.7293447
4          avg_edge_size   6.5641026
5 pairwise_participation   1.0000000

Pairwise participation is 1.0: every pair of codes co-occurs somewhere. So the projection is the complete graph, and any first-order centrality on it is near-degenerate — the same saturation that makes the first-order transition network uninformative in the three-families comparison.

deg <- rowSums(net$weights > 0)
range(deg)
[1] 8 8

Every node has degree 8. The hypergraph, meanwhile, still distinguishes the codes clearly by size and overlap structure — see hypergraph_centrality().

When to use it anyway

  • To hand a hypergraph to a tool that only accepts pairwise networks.
  • To compare a higher-order result against its first-order counterpart, and show that the higher-order structure is doing work.
  • When Chitra & Raphael’s collapse theorem applies: with edge-independent vertex weights, a random walk on the hypergraph is equivalent to one on the weighted clique expansion. In that case the projection is lossless for walk-based purposes, and the hypergraph adds nothing — which is itself worth knowing, and is why window_hypergraph()’s edge-dependent weights matter.

What to do next

  • build_hypergraph() — the inverse direction, with an explicit belief parameter.
  • hypergraph_centrality() — centrality without projecting.
  • hypergraph_measures() — the overlap structure that projection flattens.

References

  • Chitra, U., & Raphael, B. J. (2019). Random walks on hypergraphs with edge-dependent vertex weights. ICML 2019, PMLR 97, 1172-1181.
  • Agarwal, S., Branson, K., & Belongie, S. (2006). Higher order learning with graphs. ICML 2006, 17-24.
  • Tian, Y., & Zafarani, R. (2024). Higher-order network analysis methods. ACM Computing Surveys.
